strengths: Good zero-shot editing performance compared to previous STOA. The demo page shows the effective controllability of some music concepts that previous models failed to control.
The benchmark is very useful for future researchers on music editing.
The methodology of Harmonized Attention Control and Disentangled Inversion Technique is novel, which could help zero-shot editing of other domains.

The main idea of this paper—incorporating mutual self-attention, cross-attention control, and harmonic control—is sensible, even though each module is not entirely novel. The combination of these mechanisms appears effective, as results indicate that combining them enhances model performance in music editing tasks, providing useful insights.

The paper is thorough in its experimental design, including both subjective evaluations and a variety of objective experiments. The results effectively demonstrate the validity of the chosen methods for the model.
The discussion of related work is comprehensive.

To improve the music editing performance of DDIM inversion, the authors did not simply combine Cross-attention control and Mutual self-attention control; they introduced an additional Harmonic Branch to integrate these techniques. Furthermore, they proposed the Disentangled Inversion Technique. By leveraging these methods, they surpass existing music-editing methods in both objective and subjective metrics.
Introduction of the Harmonic Branch and Disentangled Inversion Technique for DDIM inversion.

The proposed method overall seems reasonably novel and well-motivated. Much space is given to explaining the facets of their method, and graphical comparison to existing methods like MusicMagus is very appreciated.
Ablations of proposed method are solid and thorough, and shows clear strengths to the design choices the authors made.
weaknesses: While the experiments are about music editing, the evaluation only uses metrics for general audio editing. Music content-related metrics like chroma distance [1] are missing.
The paper does not seem to be clear enough.

The values and effects of the hyperparameters in the paper are unclear, like $k, \tau_c, L$ and $S$. Ablation study or case study by changing these hyperparameters would be helpful to understand the model.
While the methodology seems to be general-purposed, the experiments only focus on music editing. This is okay but limits the impact of the paper a bit.

Typos and formatting errors (e.g., inconsistency use of fonts; formatting error of \hat in $\hat{M}^{\textrm{tgt}}$; $\epsilon_{c_{\textrm{tgt}}}$ should be $\epsilon_{\textrm{tgt}}$; Figure 2 notation inconsistency; Equation 9 undefined $l$; Table 6 not referenced in the appendix).
The paper needs to clarify what is meant by “rigid” and “non-rigid” tasks; no clear explanation is provided.
The terminology in the main body does not consistently maintain the focus on music editing; suggests aligning terms from “audio editing” to “music editing.”

It is debatable whether the multiple control method achieves “disentangled” control; experiments showing one control does not interfere with another are missing, making the term potentially misleading.
The description of the subjective evaluation is incomplete; details such as gender, age, music background, and musical training distribution of subjects are missing.
Hypothesis tests should be conducted for all reported results.
Insufficient or unclear validation of the effectiveness of the proposed method, directly related to the originality of this work.
Unclear motivation for incorporating the inversion process (L3 in Algorithm 2) within the problem setup where a source prompt $\mathcal{P}$ is provided.
The contribution of ZoME-Bench to the music-editing field seems somewhat limited.
The validity of the objective metrics used for evaluation remains unclear.
Given the ambiguity of these objective metrics, the experimental justification for the advantages of using the Harmonic Branch and introducing the Disentangled Inversion Technique seems insufficient.
ZoME-Bench lacks edited audio samples that define how the source samples are supposed to be edited, limiting its usefulness.
The paper's presentation quality needs revision.
The paper contains a number of grammatical errors, incorrect names of things, and incorrect citations.
The “Branch” term (line 070) is introduced without explanation.
“rigid” and “non-rigid” edits are introduced without explanation; not elucidated by figure 1.
(Line 143) “plug-in-plus” is unclear; possibly a typo for plug-and-play.
(Line 369) “ZoMo-bench” is unclear; possibly a typo from ZoME-Bench.
It should be “MedleyDB” not “MelodyDB” (line 370).
Appendix C seems to contain duplicated information.
MusicCaps has an incorrect citation on line 161; should point to Agostinelli et al.
Distinct lack of clarity in the methodological contributions and what are contributions from the authors.
Overuse of acronym-like terms makes it hard to tell what is a subset of what (e.g., Disentangled Inversion Control, Harmonized Attention Control, Disentangled Inversion Technique).
Section 3.3.1 introduces Global Attention Refinement and Local Attention Blend without clear justification or indication of novelty.
In Equation 2, a lone $M_t$ is present and it is unclear which attention map this refers to.
In equations 3/4, the threshold function takes $w_{src/tgt}$ as argument but in equation 6 it is only a function of the mask and the threshold.
Sections 3.3.1 and 3.3.2 are relatively hard to follow without intimate knowledge of past image-domain works; need more concrete examples.
In 3.3.3 (and algorithm 2), it is unclear whether “forward” refers to the forward diffusion process or the forward pass of the model; nomenclature should be fixed.
Paragraph 2 references a caption including “with noise,” which does not exist.
“MEDIC” is used without explanation of what it refers to.
The key hyperparameter $T_{start}$ is unclear how it is chosen for the proposed method and for baseline comparisons.
It is unclear how the MusicDelta section of MedleyDB was used for the task; the types of edits in this dataset are not described.
LPAPS results appear inconsistent and unusually low compared to prior work; similar inconsistencies hold for FAD, and the results for DDPM-friendly differ from the original paper.
Standard error bars are not reported for the subjective listening results; number of subjects and samples tested are not stated, making statistical significance unclear.
FAD is an odd metric for paired samples; it is unpaired, distributional, and unstable with small sample sizes, making results unstable given ZoME-Bench’s size.

The qualitative results argument is heuristic; spectrogram visualizations lack clear structural relevance, and many audio demo samples do not perform the target edit while preserving non-edited content.
The benchmark lacks ground truth information about the correctness of the edit; reliance on CLAP score assumes small text changes lead to meaningful embedding changes without support.
A model could achieve perfect benchmark scores by changing the CLAP embedding without actually editing the source audio.
The benchmark does not include edited audio samples or source-separated tracks that would provide ground truth targets.
The paper lacks a rigorous definition of “rigid” and “non-rigid” in text-based audio editing and does not justify task categorization.
Tasks such as genre, mood, rhythm, background, melody are ill-defined and do not disentangle content vs. stylistic changes, diverging from how musicians describe semantic changes.
Overall, the benchmark's utility is limited due to lack of ground truth, unclear definitions, and over-reliance on CLAP similarity.
